solution:
A primary amine is named as an alkanamine (the 'e' of the alkane replaced by 'amine'); substituents on the nitrogen itself take the locant N. The class is decided by how many carbon groups nitrogen carries.

(i) \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHNH}_2\) — Propan-2-amine; primary (1\(^\circ\)).
(ii) \(\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}_2\) — Propan-1-amine; primary (1\(^\circ\)).
(iii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{NHCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) — N-Methylpropan-2-amine; secondary (2\(^\circ\)).
(iv) \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CNH}_2\) — 2-Methylpropan-2-amine; primary (1\(^\circ\)). Nitrogen carries only one carbon group, even though that carbon is tertiary.
(v) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3\) — N-Methylaniline (N-methylbenzenamine); secondary (2\(^\circ\)).
(vi) \((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NCH}_3\) — N-Ethyl-N-methylethanamine; tertiary (3\(^\circ\)).
(vii) \(m-\text{BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2\) — 3-Bromoaniline (3-bromobenzenamine); primary (1\(^\circ\)).

(i) Methylamine (1\(^\circ\)) and dimethylamine (2\(^\circ\)) — **carbylamine (isocyanide) test.** On warming with chloroform and ethanolic KOH only the primary amine gives the extremely foul-smelling isocyanide:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\,\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CH}_3\text{NC} + 3\,\text{KCl} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Dimethylamine gives no such smell.

(ii) Secondary and tertiary amines — **Hinsberg's test** with benzenesulphonyl chloride \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl})\). A secondary amine reacts to give an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has no hydrogen on nitrogen, is therefore not acidic and stays INSOLUBLE in alkali. A tertiary amine has no N–H at all and does not react with the reagent.

(iii) Ethylamine and aniline — **azo dye test.** Aniline, an aromatic primary amine, is diazotised at 273-278 K and the diazonium salt couples with alkaline 2-naphthol to give a brilliant orange-red azo dye. Ethylamine, an aliphatic primary amine, gives an unstable diazonium salt which at once evolves nitrogen gas (brisk effervescence) and gives ethanol, so no dye forms. Simpler still: aniline with bromine water gives an immediate white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline; ethylamine gives none.

(iv) Aniline and benzylamine — treat with nitrous acid at 273-278 K. Aniline gives a stable arenediazonium salt which couples with 2-naphthol to an orange dye. In benzylamine the nitrogen is not attached to the ring, so it behaves as an aliphatic primary amine: it effervesces, releasing \(\text{N}_2\), and gives benzyl alcohol.

(v) Aniline and N-methylaniline — **carbylamine test.** Aniline is primary and gives foul-smelling phenyl isocyanide with chloroform and alcoholic KOH:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\,\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NC} + 3\,\text{KCl} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
N-Methylaniline is secondary and gives no reaction.

(i) In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is in conjugation with the benzene ring — aniline is a resonance hybrid of five structures — so the pair is delocalised and much less available to a proton; the nitrogen is also joined to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which is more electronegative than the \(sp^3\) carbon of methylamine and withdraws electron density. In methylamine the \(+\text{I}\) effect of the methyl group instead pushes electron density onto nitrogen and stabilises the methylammonium ion formed. Aniline is thus the weaker base, and a weaker base has the larger \(\text{p}K_b\).

(ii) Ethylamine dissolves because its \(-\text{NH}_2\) group forms hydrogen bonds with water and its ethyl group is too small to outweigh them. In aniline the bulky hydrophobic phenyl group dominates the molecule, and because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring the nitrogen is also a poorer hydrogen-bond acceptor. Aniline is therefore only sparingly soluble.

(iii) Methylamine is a stronger base than water, so in aqueous solution it takes a proton from water and generates hydroxide ions:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3 + \overset{-}{\text{O}}\text{H}\)
Those hydroxide ions precipitate \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) as hydrated ferric oxide:
\(2\,\text{FeCl}_3 + 6\,\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + 6\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot 3\text{H}_2\text{O} + 6\,\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\)

(iv) Nitration is carried out in a strongly acidic medium (conc. \(\text{HNO}_3\) with conc. \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)). There aniline is largely protonated to the anilinium ion, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\), in which nitrogen carries a full positive charge. The \(-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\) group is strongly electron-withdrawing and therefore meta-directing and deactivating. The mixture contains both free aniline (giving the o- and p-products) and the anilinium ion (giving the m-product), so a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline is formed.

(v) The Friedel-Crafts catalyst \(\text{AlCl}_3\) is a Lewis acid and the amine nitrogen is a Lewis base, so aniline simply forms a salt with it. Nitrogen then bears a positive charge and acts as a strong deactivating, meta-directing group, leaving the ring too electron-poor for electrophilic alkylation or acylation — and the catalyst is consumed in the process.

(vi) In an arenediazonium ion the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance, which is why such salts survive for a short time in solution at 273-278 K. An alkyldiazonium ion has no ring to delocalise the charge, so nothing stabilises it and it decomposes at once, expelling \(\text{N}_2\) — an exceptionally good leaving group — to give a carbocation.

(vii) Ammonolysis of an alkyl halide gives a MIXTURE of primary, secondary and tertiary amines together with the quaternary ammonium salt, because the amine first formed is itself a nucleophile and reacts further. In the Gabriel synthesis the phthalimide anion has a single nucleophilic nitrogen, and once it has been alkylated that nitrogen carries no hydrogen to be replaced, so exactly one alkyl group is introduced. Alkaline hydrolysis then liberates a pure primary amine, uncontaminated by higher amines.

[Textbook answer-key error in part (i), an inequality printed the wrong way round. The question asks for the compounds in order of DECREASING \(pK_b\), and the key lists them in the same sequence as the answer below but joins them with \(<\), which asserts that aniline has the SMALLEST \(pK_b\) — i.e. that it is the strongest base of the four, the reverse of the truth. The book's own Table 9.3 settles it: aniline \(9.38\), N-methylaniline \(9.30\), ethylamine \(3.29\), diethylamine \(3.00\), which is exactly the decreasing order given below. That this is a slip rather than a house convention is shown by the same key entry using \(>\) correctly in part (iv) and \(<\) correctly in parts (v) and (vi). The sequence of compounds is right in both; only the symbol is wrong. Parts (ii) to (vi) agree term for term.] (i) Decreasing order of \(\text{p}K_b\) — this is the order of INCREASING basic strength reversed, so the weakest base comes first. Aniline is weakest (lone pair delocalised into the ring); N-methylaniline is a little stronger because the \(+\text{I}\) methyl group partly offsets that; the two aliphatic amines are far stronger, and the secondary one strongest in water:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3 > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\)

(ii) Increasing order of basic strength. Both aromatic amines have the nitrogen bonded to the ring, so both are weak; the two methyl groups of N,N-dimethylaniline raise its basicity above aniline's. The aliphatic amines follow, the secondary above the primary:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2 < \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 < (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\)

(iii) Increasing order of basic strength.
(a) The \(-\text{NO}_2\) group is strongly electron-withdrawing and drains the ring and the nitrogen, while \(-\text{CH}_3\) is electron-releasing:
\(p\text{-nitroaniline} < \text{aniline} < p\text{-toluidine}\)
(b) In benzylamine the ring is insulated from nitrogen by a \(-\text{CH}_2-\) group, so the lone pair is not delocalised at all and it is by far the strongest. Between the other two, the \(+\text{I}\) methyl on nitrogen makes N-methylaniline slightly the stronger:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3 < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\)

(iv) Decreasing order of basic strength in the GAS phase. With no solvent there is no solvation of the cation, so only the electron-releasing inductive effect of the alkyl groups operates and basicity simply rises with their number:
\((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} > (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3\)

(v) Increasing order of boiling point. All three associate through intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the O–H bond is more polar and ethanol's hydrogen bonds are the strongest. Of the two amines, which have the same molar mass, the primary one has TWO N–H hydrogens available for bonding against the secondary amine's one:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH} < \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)

(vi) Increasing order of solubility in water. Solubility depends on hydrogen bonding to water and falls as the hydrophobic part grows. Aniline has a large phenyl group and a delocalised lone pair; diethylamine has two ethyl groups and one N–H; ethylamine has one ethyl group and two N–H:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} < \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)

The carbon count decides the route: cyanide adds a carbon (ascent of the series), the Hofmann bromamide degradation removes one (descent), and nitrous acid converts a primary aliphatic amine to the alcohol.

(i) Ethanoic acid into methanamine (2 C to 1 C, so a descent):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{NH}_3} \text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\)

(ii) Hexanenitrile into 1-aminopentane (6 C to 5 C, a descent):
\(\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CN} \xrightarrow[\text{partial hydrolysis}]{\overset{-}{\text{O}}\text{H}} \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\)

(iii) Methanol to ethanoic acid (1 C to 2 C, an ascent):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN (alc.)}} \text{CH}_3\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)

(iv) Ethanamine into methanamine (2 C to 1 C):
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HNO}_2} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow[\text{H}^{+}]{\text{KMnO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{NH}_3} \text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\)

(v) Ethanoic acid into propanoic acid (2 C to 3 C, an ascent):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[(\text{ii})\ \text{H}_2\text{O}]{(\text{i})\ \text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_2} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN (alc.)}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\)

(vi) Methanamine into ethanamine (1 C to 2 C):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HNO}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN (alc.)}} \text{CH}_3\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)

(vii) Nitromethane into dimethylamine — reduce, then alkylate once:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}} \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}\)

(viii) Propanoic acid into ethanoic acid (3 C to 2 C):
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{NH}_3} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HNO}_2} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow[\text{H}^{+}]{\text{KMnO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)

The three classes are distinguished by **Hinsberg's test**, which turns on how many hydrogen atoms the nitrogen still carries. The reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}\) (these days often replaced by p-toluenesulphonyl chloride). The amine is shaken with the reagent and excess aqueous KOH.

**Primary amine** — reacts to give an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{NC}_2\text{H}_5 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{HCl}\)
The hydrogen left on nitrogen is strongly acidic, because the sulphonyl group is powerfully electron-withdrawing and stabilises the anion formed. The product therefore DISSOLVES in alkali:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\overset{-}{\text{N}}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)\ \text{K}^{+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Secondary amine** — reacts to give an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl} + \text{HN}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{N}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2 + \text{HCl}\)
Here nitrogen retains no hydrogen, so the sulphonamide is not acidic and remains INSOLUBLE in alkali.

**Tertiary amine** — has no hydrogen on nitrogen to replace and does not react with the reagent at all; it simply remains as the free amine, and is recovered unchanged.

So: a product soluble in alkali indicates a primary amine, a product insoluble in alkali a secondary amine, and no reaction a tertiary amine.

A primary amine can be confirmed independently by the carbylamine test, which only primary amines give:
\(\text{R}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\,\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{R}-\text{NC} + 3\,\text{KCl} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(i) **Carbylamine reaction (isocyanide test).** An aliphatic or aromatic PRIMARY amine heated with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide gives a carbylamine (isocyanide), which has an extremely offensive smell. Secondary and tertiary amines do not respond, so the reaction is used as a test for primary amines:
\(\text{R}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\,\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{R}-\text{NC} + 3\,\text{KCl} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(ii) **Diazotisation.** The conversion of a primary AROMATIC amine into a diazonium salt by nitrous acid (generated in situ from sodium nitrite and a mineral acid) at 273-278 K:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{NaNO}_2 + 2\,\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{273-278\ \text{K}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} + \text{NaCl} + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
The low temperature is essential because the salt is unstable; it is used at once rather than stored.

(iii) **Hofmann's bromamide reaction.** An amide treated with bromine in aqueous or ethanolic sodium hydroxide gives a primary amine. An alkyl or aryl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen, so the amine has ONE CARBON LESS than the amide:
\(\text{R}-\text{CONH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 4\,\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\,\text{NaBr} + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iv) **Coupling reaction.** A diazonium salt attacks an electron-rich aromatic ring (a phenol or an arylamine) at its para position in an electrophilic substitution, retaining the diazo group. The two rings are joined through \(-\text{N}=\text{N}-\), giving an extended conjugated system, so the azo compounds are coloured and are used as dyes. With phenol in alkaline medium benzenediazonium chloride gives p-hydroxyazobenzene (an orange dye); with aniline in acidic medium it gives p-aminoazobenzene (a yellow dye).

(v) **Ammonolysis.** The cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond of an alkyl or benzyl halide by ammonia, the halogen being replaced by \(-\text{NH}_2\). It is carried out in a sealed tube at 373 K. The primary amine first formed is itself a nucleophile, so the reaction continues to the secondary and tertiary amine and finally the quaternary ammonium salt; a large excess of ammonia is used to obtain the primary amine as the main product:
\(\text{R}-\text{X} + \text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{R}-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\ \overset{-}{\text{X}} \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH}} \text{R}-\text{NH}_2\)

(vi) **Acetylation.** Replacement of a hydrogen of \(-\text{NH}_2\) or \(>\text{N}-\text{H}\) by the acetyl group, using acetyl chloride or acetic anhydride, to give an amide. It is done in the presence of a base stronger than the amine (pyridine), which removes the HCl formed and drives the equilibrium forward. It is also used to PROTECT the amino group of aniline, whose activating effect is thereby reduced so that monosubstitution can be achieved:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + (\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)

(vii) **Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.** Phthalimide with ethanolic KOH gives its potassium salt, which on heating with an alkyl halide gives the N-alkylphthalimide; alkaline hydrolysis then liberates a PURE primary amine, free of secondary and tertiary amines. Aromatic primary amines cannot be made this way, because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

(i) Nitrobenzene to benzoic acid — the ring carbon must gain a carbon, which the diazonium route supplies:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\)

(ii) Benzene to m-bromophenol — bromine must enter meta, so it is introduced while the meta-directing nitro group is still present:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow{\text{conc. HNO}_3/\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{anhyd. FeBr}_3} m\text{-bromonitrobenzene} \xrightarrow{\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}} m\text{-bromoaniline}\)
\(\xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{the diazonium chloride} \xrightarrow[283\ \text{K}]{\text{H}_2\text{O}} m\text{-bromophenol}\)

(iii) Benzoic acid to aniline — a descent by one carbon:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{NH}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)

(iv) Aniline to 2,4,6-tribromofluorobenzene — brominate first, using the amino group's activating power, then replace it by fluorine through the fluoroborate:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}} 2,4,6\text{-tribromoaniline} \xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{the diazonium chloride} \xrightarrow{\text{HBF}_4} \text{the diazonium fluoroborate} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2,4,6\text{-tribromofluorobenzene}\)

(v) Benzyl chloride to 2-phenylethanamine — one carbon is added, so the nitrile route:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN (alc.)}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\)

(vi) Chlorobenzene to p-chloroaniline — chlorine is o-/p-directing, so nitration gives mainly the para isomer, which is then reduced:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. HNO}_3/\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} p\text{-chloronitrobenzene} \xrightarrow{\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}} p\text{-chloroaniline}\)

(vii) Aniline to p-bromoaniline — direct bromination would give the 2,4,6-tribromo compound, so the amino group is first protected by acetylation:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}} \text{acetanilide} \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}} p\text{-bromoacetanilide} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} p\text{-bromoaniline}\)
The lone pair of the acetylated nitrogen is drawn towards the carbonyl oxygen, so the ring is less strongly activated and only one bromine enters.

(viii) Benzamide to toluene — the carbonyl carbon must be RETAINED and reduced to \(-\text{CH}_3\), so the amide is reduced rather than degraded:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow[(\text{ii})\ \text{H}_2\text{O}]{(\text{i})\ \text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{red P}/\text{HI}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3\)
Benzylamine is a primary ALIPHATIC amine, so nitrous acid replaces its \(-\text{NH}_2\) by \(-\text{OH}\) with loss of \(\text{N}_2\).

(ix) Aniline to benzyl alcohol — one carbon must be added to the ring and then reduced:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[(\text{ii})\ \text{H}_2\text{O}]{(\text{i})\ \text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(i) Cyanide displaces iodide to give the nitrile; partial hydrolysis stops at the amide; bromine in alkali is the Hofmann degradation, which removes one carbon.
A = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}\) (propanenitrile); B = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2\) (propanamide); C = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\) (ethanamine).

(ii) Cuprous cyanide replaces the diazonium group (Sandmeyer); the nitrile is hydrolysed to the acid; ammonia and heat give the amide.
A = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN}\) (benzonitrile); B = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\) (benzoic acid); C = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2\) (benzamide).

(iii) Cyanide gives the nitrile; \(\text{LiAlH}_4\) reduces it to the primary amine with one carbon MORE than the bromide; nitrous acid then replaces \(-\text{NH}_2\) of this aliphatic amine by \(-\text{OH}\), with loss of \(\text{N}_2\).
A = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}\) (propanenitrile); B = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\) (propan-1-amine); C = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) (propan-1-ol).

(iv) Iron and hydrochloric acid reduce the nitro group; nitrous acid at 273 K diazotises; warming the aqueous solution hydrolyses the diazonium salt to the phenol.
A = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\) (aniline); B = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\) (benzenediazonium chloride); C = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}\) (phenol).

(v) Ammonia and heat convert the acid to the amide; sodium hypobromite is the Hofmann degradation reagent and removes one carbon; nitrous acid then gives the alcohol from this primary aliphatic amine.
A = \(\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2\) (ethanamide); B = \(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\) (methanamine); C = \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) (methanol).

(vi) Reduction then diazotisation as in (iv); the diazonium salt now COUPLES with phenol instead of being hydrolysed, because the reaction is run at low temperature with an electron-rich ring present, and substitution occurs at the position para to the hydroxyl group.
A = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\) (aniline); B = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\) (benzenediazonium chloride); C = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N}=\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{OH}\) (p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye).

Work backwards from C. \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}\) with an aromatic ring is \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), aniline. Bromine with potassium hydroxide is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, so B must be the amide with ONE CARBON MORE than the amine, i.e. benzamide. An amide is obtained by heating an acid with aqueous ammonia, so A is benzoic acid.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{aq. NH}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{KOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)

A = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\), benzoic acid.
B = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2\), benzamide.
C = \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\), aniline (benzenamine).

(i) Carbylamine reaction — aniline is a primary amine:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\,\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NC} + 3\,\text{KCl} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Phenyl isocyanide, foul-smelling.

(ii) Hypophosphorous acid reduces the diazonium salt, replacing the diazonium group by hydrogen:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3 + \text{HCl}\)

(iii) Aniline is a base and first forms the salt with the acid:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\ (\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\ \text{HSO}_4^{-}\)
Anilinium hydrogensulphate. On heating this with sulphuric acid at 453-473 K it rearranges to sulphanilic acid (p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid), which exists as a zwitterion.

(iv) Ethanol also reduces the diazonium salt, and is itself oxidised to ethanal:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{N}_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{HCl}\)

(v) The amino group is a powerful activator, so bromine water substitutes at both ortho positions and the para position at once, giving a white precipitate:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 3\,\text{Br}_2\ (\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2,4,6\text{-tribromoaniline} + 3\,\text{HBr}\)

(vi) Acetylation of the amino group:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + (\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)
N-Phenylethanamide (acetanilide).

(vii) Fluoroboric acid precipitates the diazonium fluoroborate, which on heating with aqueous sodium nitrite in the presence of copper has its diazonium group replaced by \(-\text{NO}_2\):
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} \xrightarrow{\text{HBF}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \text{BF}_4^{-} \xrightarrow[\text{Cu},\ \Delta]{\text{NaNO}_2} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + \text{N}_2 + \text{NaBF}_4\)
Nitrobenzene.

The Gabriel synthesis works because the phthalimide ANION, a nucleophile, attacks the halide carbon in a nucleophilic substitution and displaces the halide ion, giving the N-alkylphthalimide.

Aryl halides do not undergo that substitution. A lone pair of the halogen is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the \(\text{C}-\text{X}\) bond acquires partial double-bond character and is shorter and stronger than in an alkyl halide; the carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised and holds the shared pair more tightly; and the ring's own \(\pi\) electron cloud repels the approaching nucleophile.

The phthalimide anion therefore cannot displace the halide from an aryl halide, no N-arylphthalimide is formed, and so aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by this route.

Nitrous acid is unstable and is prepared in situ from sodium nitrite and a mineral acid. Both classes of primary amine give a diazonium salt; what differs is whether that salt survives.

(i) Aromatic primary amines. At 273-278 K aniline gives an arenediazonium salt, in which the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance. The salt is therefore stable enough to be kept for a short time in cold solution and used at once:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{NaNO}_2 + 2\,\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{273-278\ \text{K}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} + \text{NaCl} + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(ii) Aliphatic primary amines. The alkyldiazonium salt formed has no ring over which to spread the charge, so nothing stabilises it. It decomposes as fast as it is made, expelling nitrogen quantitatively and giving the alcohol:
\(\text{R}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{HNO}_2 \rightarrow [\text{R}-\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}] \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{R}-\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{HCl}\)
Because exactly one mole of nitrogen is evolved per mole of \(-\text{NH}_2\), the reaction is used to estimate amino groups in amino acids and proteins.

(i) Acidity here means the ease with which the \(\text{N}-\text{H}\) or \(\text{O}-\text{H}\) bond releases a proton. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen (about 3.0 against 3.5), so the \(\text{N}-\text{H}\) bond is less polar and gives up its hydrogen less readily. More important, the conjugate base left behind is less stable: the negative charge on the amide ion \(\text{R}_2\overset{-}{\text{N}}\) sits on the larger, less electronegative nitrogen, whereas an alkoxide \(\text{R}\overset{-}{\text{O}}\) puts it on the smaller, more electronegative oxygen, which accommodates it far better. A less stable conjugate base means a weaker acid, so amines are less acidic than alcohols of comparable molar mass.

(ii) Boiling point here is governed by intermolecular hydrogen bonding. A primary amine, \(\text{R}-\text{NH}_2\), has TWO hydrogen atoms on nitrogen, so its molecules are extensively associated and a large amount of energy is needed to separate them. A tertiary amine, \(\text{R}_3\text{N}\), has NO hydrogen on nitrogen at all, so intermolecular hydrogen bonding is impossible and its molecules are held together only by weak van der Waals forces. Hence primary amines boil at a much higher temperature than tertiary amines of comparable molar mass. (A secondary amine, with one N–H, lies between them.)

(iii) Basicity depends on how available the lone pair on nitrogen is, and on how stable the cation formed on protonation is. In an aliphatic amine the alkyl groups release electrons \((+\text{I})\), increasing the electron density on nitrogen and dispersing the positive charge of the ammonium ion formed; the lone pair is localised on nitrogen and fully available. In an aromatic amine the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is in conjugation with the \(\pi\) system and is delocalised over the ring — aniline is a resonance hybrid of five structures — leaving it much less available to a proton. The nitrogen is also bonded to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which is more electronegative than an \(sp^3\) carbon and pulls electron density away from it. Finally, protonation costs resonance stabilisation: aniline has five resonating structures whereas the anilinium ion has only two. Aliphatic amines are therefore the stronger bases.
